claims.text: Controlled shot peening introduces compressive residual stresses into the surfaces of carbon and low-alloy steels.
Shot peening forms a surface dislocation network in carbon and low-alloy steels.
Shot-peening-induced compressive residual stresses improve the corrosion resistance of carbon and low-alloy steels.
The corrosion improvement results from enhanced adhesion and integrity of naturally forming passive oxide films.
An oxide surface layer forms through reactions with high-temperature, high-pressure water.
Untreated carbon and low-alloy steels develop a conventional passive film under the proposed nuclear-water and acidic conditions.
The passive films on untreated steels contain typical localized imperfections.
Compressive residual stresses reduce the initiation of microcracks and defects in the passive oxide layer.
Compressive residual stresses reduce the propagation of microcracks and defects in the passive oxide layer.
Reducing oxide-layer cracking and defects produces a more adherent and uniform passive film.
Greater passive-film integrity reduces localized dissolution and impedes corrosion progression.
Shot-peened samples will have lower corrosion rates and electrochemical corrosion currents than untreated samples.
Shot-peened samples will have fewer oxide-film defects and more adherent passive films than untreated samples.
The beneficial corrosion effect depends on maintenance of the induced compressive residual stresses.
Prolonged high-temperature exposure may substantially relax the induced compressive residual stresses.
Relaxation of compressive residual stress may diminish the corrosion-resistance benefit of shot peening.
The proposed mechanism applies in both simulated nuclear-water chemistry and acidic chemical-processing environments.

contradictions.description: The boundary states that the benefit is conditional on retention of compressive stress and may disappear after stress relaxation, but the falsification rule treats stress relaxation accompanied by no improvement as falsifying the hypothesis. That result is compatible with the stated boundary rather than a decisive refutation of the proposed stress-dependent mechanism.
